speaker: Elena Verna
title: 10 growth tactics that never work | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey)
question: In product growth, why does requiring an A/B test for every change backfire?
guest: If every single initiative on growth has to be an experiment, it becomes a paralyzing disease that slows down velocity, progress, and learnings, because the team becomes afraid to ship any change without a scientific readout. Data is only good if you have enough of it. If you're touching low-volume real estate that will take eight months to reach sample size, testing it makes no sense—my rule of thumb is that if we cannot collect the sample size within a month, we shouldn't A/B test it. Reserve formal experimentation for very high-traffic surfaces where even a 0.1 percent lift means millions of dollars, or for major strategic pivots that require validation before heavy follow-on investment. Everywhere else, just ship and measure pre-versus-post—with 24-hour, 7-day, 28-day, and longer-term retention readouts—and roll back if it doesn't work.

points.core: Low-volume surfaces take months to reach sample size, paralyzing shipping velocity.
points.note: Accept: requiring statistical significance on low-traffic surfaces forces long wait times (e.g., beyond a month or many months) to hit sample size, stalling shipping speed and learning. Do not credit: generic complaints that testing is bureaucratic without the sample-size/traffic mechanism.

points.core: Experiment mandates make teams afraid to ship changes without formal statistical readouts.
points.note: Accept: forcing every change through A/B tests locks teams into risk-averse paralysis where they stop trusting user intuition and refuse to ship routine improvements without scientific proof. Do not credit: anti-data platitudes that dismiss experimentation altogether.

points.core: Low-traffic changes work better as direct launches measured through pre-versus-post readouts.
points.note: Accept: reserving formal A/B tests for high-traffic surfaces or major pivots while shipping lower-volume changes directly with pre-versus-post monitoring (e.g., 24h, 7d, 28d readouts) and rollback options. Do not credit: shipping blindly without post-launch measurement.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Requiring an A/B test for every change backfires because experiments are expensive, and a blanket mandate spends that cost where it buys nothing.

Each test needs enough traffic and time to reach statistical significance. Most products lack the volume to detect small effects, so teams either wait weeks for an answer or ship on noise. Running many underpowered tests also guarantees false positives, so "wins" pile up that never show in the top-line metrics.

The mandate also distorts what gets built. Teams gravitate towards small, easily measurable tweaks and away from big bets, whose value is long-term, strategic, or hard to capture in a short-term metric. Optimising each local metric can produce a product that is incoherent or quietly worse: dark patterns often "win" tests while eroding trust and retention.

Finally, it replaces judgment with process. Obvious fixes, bug repairs, and reversible low-risk changes get delayed, velocity drops, and "the test said so" becomes a way to avoid accountability.

The better rule is to test when the uncertainty and the stakes are high, the effect is measurable, and the result would change your decision. Otherwise, ship and monitor.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Requiring an A/B test for every change traps product teams in local maxima while crippling execution speed. Because experiments favor small, isolated tweaks that produce clean readouts, strict testing mandates discourage bold, cohesive bets and step-change innovations whose value only emerges when multiple parts evolve together, or after users overcome initial change aversion.

Operationally, universal testing wastes engineering effort and scarce user traffic on obvious bug fixes, UX polish, and low-volume flows where reaching statistical significance takes weeks or is mathematically impossible, grinding shipping velocity to a halt. Worse, it biases teams toward short-term, easily measured proxy metrics—like immediate clicks or sign-ups—at the expense of harder-to-measure long-term retention, user trust, and brand coherence. Over time, stacking dozens of locally "winning" micro-optimizations introduces unmeasured interaction effects and degrades overall product craft, leaving behind a fragmented experience that erodes user loyalty even as individual experiment dashboards look green.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Requiring an A/B test for every change backfires because testing has real costs that grow with scale, and a blanket rule spends them where they buy nothing. Most products don't have enough traffic to detect the small effects typical changes produce. Teams end up running underpowered tests that drag on for weeks, finish inconclusive, or turn up false positives that get shipped as "wins." Velocity drops because every tweak waits in a queue for experiment slots and analysis. Incentives also get distorted. Teams start favoring small, easily measured tweaks like button colors and copy over bold, strategic bets whose value is long-term, spread out, or hard to isolate, such as brand, trust, infrastructure, or new product lines. Short test windows reward novelty effects and local optimizations that can hurt retention or user experience over time. A test-everything rule also lets teams hand judgment to the dashboard, so nobody owns the decision, and obvious fixes like bugs, legal requirements, and clear usability problems get needlessly delayed. A better approach is to save rigorous experiments for high-stakes, uncertain, reversible decisions that have enough sample size, and to rely on judgment, qualitative research, and staged rollouts for the rest.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Requiring an A/B test for every change backfires because it trades speed, judgment, and strategic ambition for an illusion of rigor. Designing, instrumenting, running, and analyzing experiments carries real engineering and opportunity costs; forcing low-risk bug fixes, obvious usability improvements, or minor copy updates through that pipeline slows shipping dramatically without meaningfully reducing risk.

It also collides with statistical reality. Many surfaces lack the traffic to detect small effects quickly, so testing every tweak produces underpowered, inconclusive results that either stall decisions or invite peeking and false positives. Worse, a test-everything mandate biases teams toward local maxima. Because isolated, short-term changes are easiest to measure, teams optimize buttons and funnels while avoiding cohesive redesigns, brand investments, or long-term platform bets whose payoffs don't show up in a two-week window. Strong growth teams reserve A/B tests for high-impact, uncertain, or hard-to-reverse decisions, and ship obvious improvements directly.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Requiring an A/B test for every change makes it harder to run the experiments that matter. Every test takes time to build, monitor, and interpret, and draws on limited traffic. For small changes or products with few users, a test can run for weeks and still leave the team unsure whether the change helped. Meanwhile, straightforward fixes sit in the queue.

A blanket rule also shapes what teams choose to build. It favors changes that can move a metric quickly and makes longer-term work, such as improving accessibility or reliability, harder to justify.

Use A/B tests when the impact is uncertain, the decision matters, and there’s enough traffic to get a meaningful result. For obvious bugs and low-risk, reversible changes, ship and monitor.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Requiring an A/B test for every change makes sense only if every decision is worth the cost of testing. A typo fix can wait weeks for a result, and the improvement may be too small to detect even when it matters to users. Meanwhile, the test consumes traffic and engineering time that could answer a more consequential question.

A blanket rule also changes what teams build. If every idea needs a measurable lift to ship, teams gravitate toward tweaks that move a metric quickly. They have less incentive to pursue improvements whose benefits accumulate over time.

A/B tests earn their cost when the outcome is uncertain, the result could change the decision, and there’s enough traffic to detect a meaningful effect. For low-risk, reversible changes, shipping and monitoring is often the better choice.
